events/directory-for-public-worship-1645: Parliament abolishes the Book of Common Prayer and authorises the Westminster Assembly’s Directory, which gives rubrics rather than set prayers and abolishes holy days other than the Lord’s Day; Christmas observance is banned in 1647.
Puritan objections to set forms and ceremonies
Restoration of the Prayer Book in 1662
events/union-of-uzhhorod-1646/summary: Sixty-three Orthodox priests of the Mukachevo region of Habsburg Hungary professed union with Rome in the castle chapel of Uzhhorod (24 April 1646), keeping their Byzantine liturgy and married clergy. It is the founding act of the Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church.
events/union-of-uzhhorod-1646/causes/0: Habsburg and Counter-Reformation support for church union
events/union-of-uzhhorod-1646/causes/1: Hopes of equal status and privileges with Latin clergy
events/union-of-uzhhorod-1646/consequenc: Soviet liquidation of the church in 1949 and revival in 1989
Ruthenian emigration to the United States
events/peace-of-westphalia-1648/summary: Treaties at Münster and Osnabrück ended the Thirty Years' War, recognised Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism in the empire and fixed confessional boundaries as of 1624. Pope Innocent X protested in vain, signalling the decline of papal political power.
events/peace-of-westphalia-1648/causes/0: Exhaustion after three decades of war
events/quaker-movement-1652/title: George Fox and the rise of the Quakers
events/quaker-movement-1652/summary: After his vision on Pendle Hill, George Fox preached to about a thousand Seekers at Firbank Fell, launching the Religious Society of Friends. Quakers taught the Inward Light of Christ in every person, rejected clergy, sacraments and oaths, and endured severe persecution.
events/quaker-movement-1652/causes/0: Radical sects of the Civil War era
events/coonan-cross-oath-1653/summary: Thousands of St Thomas Christians, holding a rope tied to a leaning cross at Mattancherry, swore not to submit to the Portuguese Jesuit hierarchy. The revolt led to the division between the Catholic Syro-Malabar community and the Malankara church, which in 1665 received Syriac Orthodox ties.
events/coonan-cross-oath-1653/causes/1: Arrest of a bishop sent from the East
events/great-ejection-1662/summary: Under the Act of Uniformity, some 2,000 English ministers who would not accept the revised Book of Common Prayer and episcopal ordination were ejected on St Bartholomew's Day 1662. Puritan Dissenters, including Richard Baxter, became Nonconformists outside the established church.
events/great-ejection-1662/causes/0: Restoration of the monarchy and bishops
events/great-ejection-1662/consequences/: Persecution under the Clarendon Code until 1689
events/mar-gregorios-arrives-kerala-1665: Syriac Orthodox bishop arrives in Malankara

Mar Gregorios Abdul Jaleel, a Syriac Orthodox bishop from Jerusalem, came to Kerala and regularised the episcopal consecration of Mar Thoma I. The Malankara church thus adopted the West Syriac liturgy and Miaphysite Christology, joining the Oriental Orthodox family.
Coonan Cross Oath and search for a bishop
Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian churches
events/nikon-reforms-old-believers-1666/: Nikon's reforms and the Old Believer schism

Patriarch Nikon conformed Russian rites to contemporary Greek usage — three-finger sign of the cross, revised books. The Great Moscow Council of 1666–67 deposed Nikon but upheld the reforms and anathematised resisters; the Old Believers, led by Archpriest Avvakum, suffered persecution and some communities chose mass self-immolation.
Desire for liturgical uniformity with the Greeks
Raskol (schism): Old Believer communities to this day
events/synod-of-jerusalem-1672/summary: Patriarch Dositheos of Jerusalem convened a synod at Bethlehem that repudiated the Calvinist confession attributed to Cyril Lucaris and defined Orthodox teaching on Scripture and tradition, free will, seven mysteries and the Eucharistic change (using the term metousiosis).
events/synod-of-jerusalem-1672/causes/0: Catholic and Protestant attempts to claim Orthodox support
events/synod-of-jerusalem-1672/consequen: Orthodox confessional statement of the 'Western captivity' period
events/pietism-pia-desideria-1675/summar: Philipp Jakob Spener's preface 'Pia Desideria' called Lutherans to more intensive Bible study in small groups (collegia pietatis), lay priesthood, practical Christianity and edifying preaching. Pietism spread through Halle and influenced Moravians, Methodists and modern evangelicalism.
events/pietism-pia-desideria-1675/causes: Devastation of the Thirty Years' War
events/revocation-of-nantes-1685/title: Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
events/revocation-of-nantes-1685/summary: Louis XIV's Edict of Fontainebleau outlawed Protestantism in France. Some 200,000 Huguenots fled to the Netherlands, Prussia, England, Switzerland and South Africa; those who remained worshipped secretly in the 'Church of the Desert'.
events/revocation-of-nantes-1685/causes/: Absolutist pursuit of 'one king, one law, one faith'
events/quietism-condemned-1687/title: Innocent XI condemns Molinos and quietism
events/quietism-condemned-1687/summary: In the bull Coelestis Pastor (20 November 1687) Innocent XI condemned 68 propositions attributed to Miguel de Molinos, who had abjured publicly and was sentenced to life imprisonment. The French sequel led to the condemnation of 23 propositions from Fénelon’s Maxims of the Saints in 1699.
events/quietism-condemned-1687/causes/1: Fear that it undermined vocal prayer, sacraments and moral effort
events/quietism-condemned-1687/consequen: Made Catholic authorities wary of mystical prayer for two centuries
Guyon and Molinos found readers among Protestant Pietists and Quakers
events/act-of-toleration-1689/summary: After the Glorious Revolution, Parliament allowed Trinitarian Protestant Dissenters — Presbyterians, Congregationalists, Baptists and Quakers — to worship in licensed meeting houses, though they remained excluded from public office and universities. Catholics and Unitarians were not covered.
events/act-of-toleration-1689/causes/1: Need for Protestant unity against James II
events/scottish-episcopacy-abolished-168: Abolition of episcopacy in the Church of Scotland

After the Revolution of 1688, the Scottish bishops refused to swear allegiance to William and Mary. Parliament abolished episcopacy in 1689 and re-established Presbyterian government in 1690; the episcopalian clergy and laity who remained loyal formed what became the Scottish Episcopal Church.
Nonjuring Scottish Episcopal Church, under penal laws especially after 1746
Consecration of Samuel Seabury for America (1784)
events/salem-witch-trials-1692/summary: In Salem Village and neighbouring towns in Puritan Massachusetts about 200 people were accused of witchcraft on the testimony of afflicted girls and “spectral evidence”; nineteen were hanged and one man, Giles Corey, was pressed to death. Ministers including Increase Mather criticised the evidence, and the trials ended in 1693; judge Samuel Sewall publicly repented in 1697.
events/salem-witch-trials-1692/causes/0: Village factionalism and frontier war trauma
events/salem-witch-trials-1692/consequen: Discredited spectral evidence and witch prosecution in New England
Public repentance by jurors and Sewall; later legislative exonerations (1711, 1957, 2001, 2022)
Became an enduring symbol of moral panic
events/kangxi-edict-of-toleration-1692/s: Grateful for Jesuit service in astronomy, diplomacy and medicine, the Kangxi Emperor issued an edict permitting Christian worship throughout China. It marked the high point of the Jesuit mission before the Chinese Rites controversy reversed imperial favour.
events/amish-division-1693/title: Amish division from the Swiss Brethren
events/amish-division-1693/summary: Jacob Ammann, an Anabaptist elder in Alsace, called for stricter shunning (Meidung) of the excommunicated, more frequent communion with foot-washing and plain dress. The disagreement with Hans Reist's party produced the Amish, who emigrated to Pennsylvania from the 1730s.
events/kimpa-vita-antonian-movement-1704: Kimpa Vita and the Antonian movement in Kongo

Beatriz Kimpa Vita, a young Kongolese noblewoman, claimed to be possessed by St Anthony and taught that Jesus and Mary were Kongolese, calling for the reunification of the war-torn kingdom at São Salvador. Capuchin missionaries denounced her; she was burned as a heretic in 1706. She is often seen as a forerunner of African-initiated Christianity.
Civil war and abandonment of the capital
Reoccupation of São Salvador by Pedro IV
events/chinese-rites-controversy-1704/ti: Papal ban on the Chinese Rites
events/chinese-rites-controversy-1704/su: After decades of dispute between Jesuits and Dominicans/Franciscans, Pope Clement XI condemned Confucian and ancestral rites (1704; bull Ex illa die, 1715), and Benedict XIV's Ex quo singulari (1742) closed debate. The Kangxi Emperor responded by restricting missions; the ban was lifted only in 1939.
events/chinese-rites-controversy-1704/ca: Disagreement over accommodation of Chinese culture
events/tranquebar-mission-1706/summary: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, Halle Pietists sent by the Danish king, began the first Protestant mission in India. Ziegenbalg learned Tamil, studied Hindu thought and translated the New Testament into Tamil (1714).
events/schwarzenau-baptisms-1708/title: First Brethren baptisms in the Eder at Schwarzenau
events/schwarzenau-baptisms-1708/summary: Eight Radical Pietists led by Alexander Mack, sheltering in the tolerant county of Sayn-Wittgenstein, baptised one another by threefold forward immersion in the river Eder in 1708. They intended to restore the New Testament church; their opponents called them Dunkers (from tunken, 'to dip').
events/schwarzenau-baptisms-1708/causes/: Radical Pietist rejection of state churches
Reading of Anabaptist and Pietist writers, including Gottfried Arnold
Persecution of separatists in the Palatinate
events/schwarzenau-baptisms-1708/consequ: Origin of the Schwarzenau Brethren (Church of the Brethren and related bodies)
Migration to Pennsylvania from 1719, with the Germantown congregation formed in 1723
Later branches: Old German Baptist Brethren (1881), Brethren Church (1883), Grace Brethren
events/unigenitus-1713/summary: Clement XI condemned 101 propositions from Pasquier Quesnel's moral reflections on the New Testament, targeting Jansenism, the Augustinian movement associated with Cornelius Jansen, Port-Royal and Pascal. The bull split the French church for decades; Jansenist sympathisers later founded the Church of Utrecht.
events/unigenitus-1713/consequences/1: Origins of the Old Catholic Church of Utrecht (1723)
events/marrow-controversy-1718/title: Marrow controversy in the Church of Scotland
events/marrow-controversy-1718/summary: The republication of The Marrow of Modern Divinity (1645), commended by Thomas Boston, provokes the General Assembly to condemn it (1720) as antinomian; twelve "Marrow men" protest (1721). The debate over the free offer of the gospel feeds the Secession of 1733.
events/marrow-controversy-1718/causes/1: Disputes over legal preparation for grace
events/marrow-controversy-1718/consequen: Lasting Scottish debate over the free offer
